terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation: aliquem aliquā rē spoliāre
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.37: Apollōnium omnī argentō spoliāstī (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: beat up, handle roughly; Traupman’s word for “mug”
evidence: Ter. Ad. 1.2.9: ipsum dominum atque omnem familiam mulcāvit usque ad mortem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically mulcāre is to beat, cudgel, maltreat (Plautus, Cicero); it says nothing of robbing.

phrases.latin: Istī latrōnēs macellārium omnī argentō ējus spoliāvērunt.
phrases.english: Those robbers robbed the grocer of all his money.

sources: Lewis & Short: spolio · Lewis & Short: rapio · Lewis & Short: mulco
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 191, 196.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
